name: Biomarker tracking and sharing

card.summary: Regularly measuring dozens to 100+ blood, body and aging markers, and sometimes publishing the results, so people can tune sleep, diet, training and skin and body-composition habits that show in how they look.
card.note: Lab results can be hard to interpret without clinician input, and some markers used in longevity circles are research tools rather than clinical tests.

quick.overview:
Biomarker tracking means measuring things like blood panels, hormones, inflammation markers, resting heart rate, body composition and epigenetic aging scores over time. People who follow it want to see how habits move the numbers and, through them, how they age, train and look.

Some practitioners share their data publicly. The best-known example is entrepreneur Bryan Johnson, whose Blueprint protocol tracked more than 100 measures and who has posted results including a DunedinPACE aging-pace score. The appearance link is indirect: markers are used to guide sleep, nutrition, training and hormone-related decisions that affect skin, body composition and visible aging.
quick.how: Practitioners typically schedule repeat blood tests, wearable readings and body scans, log them in spreadsheets or apps, and compare results with earlier values after changing a habit or supplement. Some publish dashboards or posts so others can see their numbers. Forum users on T Nation mention tracking hormones such as SHBG and estrogen, resting heart rate and training volume alongside their routines.
quick.risks: Interpreting panels without medical training can lead to over- or misreading normal variation, and more testing does not by itself change outcomes. Privacy is a concern when health data are posted publicly or held by apps. Critics of the longevity version, such as pharmacology professor Moshe Szyf, have said science cannot yet deliver the results claimed from such protocols.

lead: Biomarker tracking and sharing is a practice in which people measure large numbers of physiological markers on a repeating schedule and, in some cases, make the results public. Markers can include blood chemistry, hormones, inflammatory markers, heart-rate measures, body composition and DNA-methylation scores such as DunedinPACE, which estimates the pace of biological aging [1]. In appearance-focused communities it is used as a feedback loop: people adjust sleep, diet, training, skincare and supplements and check whether their numbers and visible aging move in the direction they want.

The practice descends from the quantified self movement, whose name Wired editors Gary Wolf and Kevin Kelly are credited with proposing in San Francisco in 2007, describing it as a collaboration of users and tool makers sharing an interest in self-knowledge through self-tracking [2]. The public-biomarker form was popularized by entrepreneur Bryan Johnson, who announced Project Blueprint in October 2021, was reported to track more than 100 health measures by 2023, and has shared his biomarker data publicly since 2023 [1].

Research relevant to the practice is mostly about the tools: reviews describe telomere-based and other biological-aging biomarkers as part of an emerging longevity medicine [3] and optical and wearable sensors for non-invasive biomarker monitoring [4][5]. No published trial has tested whether tracking and publicly sharing a personal panel changes appearance.

chain: Measure blood, hormone, aging and body-composition markers repeatedly
Link changes in sleep, diet, training or supplements to the numbers
Adjust habits that affect skin, physique and visible aging
angle.text: People use repeat testing to see which habits improve markers they associate with looking younger and leaner, then keep the ones that move the numbers. Publishing results lets others compare and, as proponents describe it, adds accountability.

infobox: Blood panels, hormones, inflammation, heart rate, body composition, DunedinPACE [1]
Varies; Johnson's protocol was reported at about $2 million a year in 2023 [1]

paras: Practitioners define a set of markers, test them at intervals and record the results over time. The set can range from a handful of routine blood values to more than 100 measures including organ function, hormones, epigenetic age and imaging. Tools include lab panels, wearables, home tests and emerging sweat and skin sensors, an area that reviews describe as moving toward non-invasive biomarker monitoring [4][5].

Self-tracking with wearable sensors dates to the 1970s, and the quantified self label was proposed in 2007; the first international conference took place in Mountain View, California, in May 2011 [2].

Bryan Johnson's Project Blueprint, announced in October 2021, brought the idea of publishing a full dataset to a wide audience. Since 2023 he has posted his biomarker data and taken part in competitive biohacking with others, an approach he credits to co-founder Kate Tolo; in 2025 he reported a DunedinPACE score of 0.503 [1]. Blueprint later launched a subscription offering and sells products based on his protocol [1].

Appearance communities discuss markers in two ways. Hormone and body-composition panels guide training and physique decisions; T Nation users, for example, discuss SHBG, estrogen and training metrics such as resting heart rate and volume personal records when evaluating routines [6][7]. Aging-clock and inflammation markers are followed by people interested in slowing visible aging, on the premise that lower biological-aging pace tracks with a younger look.

Proponents say that frequent measurement turns guesses into feedback and that public sharing creates accountability and lets others replicate protocols. Critics and researchers urge caution: Moshe Szyf of McGill University has expressed skepticism that science can yet produce the results Johnson claims, and longevity scientist Andrew Steele has argued that no amount of such practices can change a person's genes [1]. Critiques of quantified self in general include data privacy, an emphasis on collecting rather than interpreting data, and the burden of constant monitoring [2].

No studies found on tracking and sharing personal biomarker panels as a practice for appearance outcomes. Related literature reviews the underlying measurements, including telomere-based biological-aging biomarkers in longevity medicine [3] and sweat and optical sensors for biomarker detection [4][5].

timeline.event: Gary Wolf and Kevin Kelly credited with proposing the term quantified self [2].
First international Quantified Self conference held in Mountain View, California [2].
Johnson begins sharing biomarker data publicly; protocol reported to track over 100 measures [1].
Johnson reports a DunedinPACE score of 0.503 [1].
